persons.name: A Filer
persons.note: THE 1835 POLL LIST AND A SECOND INDEPENDENT SOURCE. Read from newspaper_1833_1835, poll_1835. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1a), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. newspaper_1833_1835 names this person at Chicago by 4 March 1834 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Poll list of 1835 — “Filer, A.” (poll_1835_023, line 308). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Filer' agrees with the entry's forenames; 2 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

persons.name: J. Garland
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED MAN ON A RECONSTRUCTED ROOF. The papers name him and this household's dwelling does not: what is attested is the person and his trade, and what remains the reconstruction's is everything about where he lived. He is printed as 'J. GARLAND' and the corpus reads his trade as cooper. Cited at the Democrat of 11 June 1834, column 11. THIS ROOF DID NOT COME FROM HIS RECORD. The household was raised by the occupation census because the town of 3,265 people in 398 dwellings needed a cooper and no documented one was available; the register (data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json, action `replace_invented`) is what says one now is. The dwelling's existence, position and footprint are unchanged and still conjectural, and nothing here claims he slept in it — only that the town's need for this trade is met by a man the papers name rather than by one this project invented. The invented name this record used to carry, and its name_basis block, are retired: an invented name is not kept beside a documented one. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1); the placement is L205. He is placed nowhere in particular by his own record, which is the condition of taking ANY roof of his trade — a man the papers put on a named street takes only a roof the plat stands on that street (T-0367), and one they place somewhere this scene cannot honour is refused outright. READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry.

residents.research_note: RECONSTRUCTED HOUSEHOLD - fourth of 4 cooper households in this layer, in the north division. A TOWN PACKING THOUSANDS OF HOGS A SEASON NEEDS COOPERS, AND THIS DATASET HELD NONE. Andreas records that Clybourne packed some 250 head of cattle and about 2,000 hogs in the season of 1833, that George W. Dole packed a further 250 cattle and 1,000 hogs at the same place, and that the Newberry & Dole house on the South Branch packed 300 cattle and 1,400 hogs in 1834 (scan p. 1151). Packed provisions travel in barrels and barrels are made by coopers. The documented layer holds a packer, two slaughter-houses and not one cooper. Four cooper households are inferred against the schedule's six W3 cooper, wagon or wheelwright shops. METHOD: the count comes from the occupation census in data/reconstruction/1835_inferred_household_programme.json, which calibrates every trade against three things this project already holds - the 1835 town census (3,265 people, 398 dwellings), Andreas's roster of the fall of 1833 (about fifty named people, most with a trade, in a settlement of some 350), and the reconstruction specification's roof schedule, whose workshop and store family targets are treated as the ceiling on a trade rather than as its measure. Every count is stated NET of the documented layer: this dataset infers a tradesman only where it cannot name one. RETIRED AN INVENTED NAME (T-0264). This household was raised by the occupation census and named from the invented-name pools. The newspaper register matched it to J. Garland, a documented cooper the corpus names 1 time(s) and places nowhere in particular, and he now holds the roof. What changed is WHO: the argument for the household, its dwelling and its position are untouched and still the reconstruction's, and the person's grade is `inferred` — a real man with reconstructed details — rather than `attested`, which would claim the dwelling too. tools/replace_invented_residents.py derives this deal and prints every candidate it refused. T-0489: reconstructed occupancy retired; evidence-based person retained and unplaced.

No figure is drawn (L1). THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Page, Miss Eleanor H. | Profession. | April 2, 1884.” (second_presb_0277, printed page 169), admitted 1884-04-02 by profession. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Page' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins E. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

citations.citation: Chicago · July 1835: Building Inventory and Architectural Reconstruction Specification. Prepared for Kevin Haas, August 2026.
what_it_supplies: A 665-roof production target with independently reconcilable group, district, level, and construction totals.
Thirty-five architectural family definitions with dimensional and massing bands.
District character, spacing, variation, finish, and chronology constraints for a July 1835 reconstruction.
A required distinction between named documentary landmarks and anonymous inferred infill.
what_it_does_not_supply: A surviving July 1835 building census or parcel-by-parcel roof register.
Exact locations, dimensions, appearance, occupants, or construction dates for anonymous roofs.
Authority to replace stronger building-specific evidence already represented in the dataset.

citations.citation: The first Chicago Catholic church register — Father John Mary Irenaeus St. Cyr's marriage register and his death and burial page — as printed and annotated in the *Illinois Catholic Historical Review*, vol. 4 (July 1921 - April 1922), and republished in two pages by the Genealogy Trails Transcription Team. 128 dated marriages of 1834-1839, each naming groom, bride, witnesses and officiating priest, and 11 deaths and burials of June 1834 to March 1837.

transcribes.work: The first Chicago Catholic church record, kept by Father J. M. I. St. Cyr from 1833 and continued by Fathers Bernard Schaeffer and Timothy O'Meara to 1839
transcribes.note: THE ORIGINAL, and nobody in this project has seen it. What is read here is a 1921-22 article that prints the marriage entries and the death entries and comments on them. The article itself says the death record 'is contained on a single page' of the book.

transcribes.work: Illinois Catholic Historical Review, vol. 4 (July 1921 - April 1922)
transcribes.note: The layer actually read, at one further remove: the Genealogy Trails team transcribed these two pages out of the Review and this project read the transcription. Every record citing this source is graded transcription_mediated, twice over.

what_it_supplies: 128 marriages at Chicago (125 of them) between 1834 and 1839, each dated, and each naming its witnesses BY NAME — 513 named readings of people standing at a named place on a named day
six marriages IN THE SCENE YEAR, which with their witnesses put twenty named people in Chicago on five days of 1835
eleven deaths and burials, four of them in 1835, including the death of Thomas Owen, agent of the Indians, at Chicago on 15 October 1835
the register's own arithmetic — 22 St. Cyr marriages, 18 Schaeffer, 87 O'Meara, 1 Plunkett — which verifies any reading of it without the book
the dates bounding each priest's time at Chicago, which is what makes an unsigned entry attributable
the Irish, French and German Catholic population of the town, which is the part the poll books and letter lists reach least well
what_it_does_not_supply: any address, lot, dwelling or workplace — the register places nobody anywhere in the town
any age, except for three infants and one nine-year-old on the death page
the baptisms. The article tallies 282 of them by these same priests and prints none; that register is T-0503's object and is not in this source
residence. A marriage at Chicago on a day of 1835 is presence on that day, and presence is not residence
reliable spelling. The article says so itself: a French and German priest writing Irish and English names, and an Irish priest writing French and German ones
